editions.title: Musk floats Tesla-SpaceX merger; CoreWeave slides on GPU price rise
editions.notification: Musk says Tesla and SpaceX merger is being assessed, with special committees formed. Nothing agreed yet.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is Elon Musk's confirmation that Tesla and SpaceX have each formed special committees to assess a possible merger. Musk stressed that nothing has been agreed. Tesla is valued at about $1.5tn and SpaceX at $2tn, which would make it the largest merger on record. Any deal would need Tesla shareholder approval from a majority of all outstanding shares, a hurdle Musk himself called high. Critics argue it would dilute shareholders, and regulators may take a close look.

AI infrastructure was under pressure. CoreWeave shares fell below $60, their lowest since May 2025, after a report said the company had raised hourly GPU prices by a further 10% on top of a July rise of about 25%. The firm owes roughly $50bn, and some bond yields have topped 15%. Rising inflation has raised the prospect of a Federal Reserve rate hike, which weighs on borrowing-heavy AI firms. Nvidia is reportedly in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid, an Australian AI cloud firm that pulled its IPO, a sign it still backs neoclouds.

Supermicro gave a strong preliminary update, with quarterly revenue of $18.5bn to $19.5bn against earlier guidance of $14.5bn to $15.5bn, though the figures are unaudited. Elsewhere, Microsoft's next Xbox plans, including a 2027 handheld, a 2028 console called Project Helix and a possible à la carte Game Pass, remain unconfirmed rumours.

top_stories.title: Musk says Tesla and SpaceX merger is under assessment
top_stories.summary: Musk said both companies have formed special committees to look at a possible merger, which would be the largest ever at about $3.5tn combined. He stressed nothing is agreed and that a Tesla shareholder vote would be a high hurdle. Analysts flag regulatory scrutiny and the mix of cars, robots, rockets and satellites involved.

top_stories.title: CoreWeave shares fall below $60 on fresh GPU price hike
top_stories.summary: CoreWeave touched its lowest level since May 2025 after reports of a further 10% rise in hourly GPU pricing. The company owes about $50bn and some bonds yield above 15%, while possible Fed rate hikes add pressure on borrowing-heavy AI infrastructure firms.

top_stories.title: Supermicro flags revenue well above guidance
top_stories.summary: Supermicro expects quarterly revenue of $18.5bn to $19.5bn, far above its earlier $14.5bn to $15.5bn guidance, with gross margin also higher. The figures are unaudited and the auditor has not reviewed them, and the company remains under investigation over AI servers allegedly smuggled to China.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly in talks to back Firmus after IPO pulled
top_stories.summary: Nvidia is said to be discussing an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid, which abandoned its IPO. The talks suggest Nvidia will keep funding neocloud providers, though critics question how far the sector relies on vendor financing.

top_stories.title: US utilities make AI data centres prove they are real
top_stories.summary: Utilities are raising rates, lengthening contracts and demanding collateral to weed out speculative data-centre projects. Wood Mackenzie expects only about 28% of 1,066GW of requested grid connections to be served, a sign that AI power demand may be overstated.

rumour_watch.note: Xbox Project Helix pricing of $1,200 to $1,800 and a 2028 launch come from a Fortune-cited report; plausible given memory costs, but Microsoft has not confirmed any figures.
A report that OpenAI is raising $30bn would be significant, but the feed gives no investor or valuation detail, so treat it as unverified.
The Galaxy S27 lineup without a Pro model rests on screen protector leaks; earlier Pro rumours did not materialise, so caution is warranted.
A $150bn private equity approach for Xbox is based on a single thin report with a 15% likelihood rating and little detail, so it looks weak.

editions.title: Anthropic and Nscale in $45bn talks; Anthropic IPO chatter grows
editions.notification: Anthropic and Nscale reportedly in talks on a $45bn compute deal. Here's what we know.
editions.intro:
The biggest story in the last 24 hours is a reported $45 billion cloud computing deal under discussion between AI developer Anthropic and Nvidia-backed Nscale. Bloomberg, Reuters and others all report that talks are under way, but no terms, timing or confirmation have come from either company. If it goes ahead, it would be a major commitment of computing capacity and a notable signal for AI infrastructure spending, though talks could still change or fail.

Anthropic is also back in the headlines over its possible listing. Bloomberg reports that former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt holds roughly a 1% stake, bought in the 2021 Series A, and that IPO marketing could start as early as the week of 9 November. Neither Schmidt nor Anthropic has commented, and the claims remain unverified. Sea Ltd's reported move into enterprise cloud and a possible fintech listing also points to companies trying to find new growth.

Elsewhere, Google said four Gemini agents completed Minecraft without human help, and Arm made performance claims against AMD's server chips that rest on modelled projections. A tipped Apple autumn event and a record $5.7 billion patent verdict against Apple add to the news flow. A South Korean data centre builder's 33% stock fall on debut is a reminder that investors are growing wary of stretched AI valuations.

top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports talks between Nscale and Anthropic on a cloud computing deal worth about $45 billion. A deal of this size would be a major compute commitment to a leading AI developer, though talks may still fail.

top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports Schmidt's stake dates from a 2021 Series A investment, with a private fair value of $1.8 to $2 trillion cited. Anthropic reportedly plans IPO marketing as early as November, but neither party has commented and the figures are unverified.

editions.title: Nscale loses Microsoft anchor as AI stocks wobble
editions.notification: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale's Essex data centre as AI infrastructure stocks slide. Here's what it means.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the period is a setback for Nscale, the British AI infrastructure firm preparing a New York listing. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out as anchor tenant of its Loughton data centre in Essex, reportedly because grid officials said power would not arrive until the 2030s. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and is exploring alternative power. The timing is awkward: Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts, and the reported $35bn valuation now faces scrutiny. The report also lands in a broader cooling of AI infrastructure sentiment, with a separate report finding at least 47 AI infrastructure projects hit setbacks this year.

Markets are feeling the same nerves. Japanese stocks fell at the open as a chip-led tech selloff deepened on doubts about the AI trade, and a Korean pension fund reportedly lost about $137bn after Samsung and SK Hynix slid. Commentators expect Magnificent Seven earnings to test whether hyperscaler AI spending holds up. Chinese data showed growth of 4.5% in the third quarter, with AI-related exports offsetting weak domestic demand and a property slump, which gives Beijing room for support measures.

Elsewhere, Apple dominated the rumour mill: reports point to touchscreen MacBooks and an OLED iPad mini arriving around 6 November, and a robotic 360-degree HomeView display, though none of this is confirmed. Its new foldable iPhone Duo is in heavy demand, with walk-in stock reportedly unlikely on launch day. Google unveiled a Gemini 4 agent team that completed Minecraft autonomously, while Meta said a Claude-linked tool wrongly suspended a protest group's Instagram account.

top_stories.summary: The Telegraph reports Microsoft has dropped its anchor role at Nscale's Loughton site, citing grid delays into the 2030s. Nscale says it remains committed and is seeking alternative power. The news lands just after its New York IPO filing, with Microsoft and Anthropic making up about 85% of contracts.

top_stories.summary: Japanese stocks fell at the open as chip names led declines, with investors questioning the viability of the AI trade. The feed gave no index levels, but the move follows a weak week for AI infrastructure names. Magnificent Seven earnings are seen as the next test.

top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports South Korea's main pension fund lost 182 trillion won as Samsung and SK Hynix shares fell. The scale shows how dependent the fund is on its largest chipmakers. It underlines the market risk from the current chip slide.

top_stories.title: China's Q3 growth edges up to 4.5% on AI exports
top_stories.summary: China grew 4.5% in the third quarter, the bottom of its target range, with AI-related chip exports offsetting weak domestic spending. Property investment fell more than 20% in the first nine months. Beijing has announced support measures, giving policymakers room to act.

top_stories.summary: POLITICO reports Anthropic has privately offered lawmakers a draft frontier AI bill allowing federal halts only for imminent, severe risks. It would give Commerce sole halt power and override some state laws. The move fuels debate over AI firms writing their own rules.

top_stories.summary: The CMA proposes designating Microsoft with Strategic Market Status in business software, citing switching difficulty for around 20 million UK users. Possible remedies include changes to bundling, licensing and interoperability. Microsoft says its products are open and it will keep engaging.

editions.title: Nscale loses Microsoft anchor as AI infrastructure jitters deepen
editions.notification: Microsoft reportedly walks away from Nscale's Essex data centre weeks before its New York IPO.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a setback for Nscale, the British AI infrastructure firm. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out as anchor tenant of its Loughton data centre in Essex, where grid power is reportedly not due until the 2030s. The news lands just after Nscale filed for a New York IPO under the ticker NSCL, with a float that could value it at up to $35bn. Microsoft and Anthropic make up about 85% of its contracts, so investors will watch delivery schedules closely. Nscale says it remains committed to Loughton and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. Microsoft has not commented.

The wider backdrop is a broad selloff in AI-linked shares. Japanese stocks fell as chip names led declines, Korean markets were hit hard, and South Korea's main pension fund reportedly lost about $137bn. Concern about whether AI spending will pay off also weighed on Oracle, Nvidia and neocloud peers. Analysts say Magnificent Seven earnings may test whether hyperscaler spending confidence holds. Meanwhile, the OpenAI Stargate project reportedly faces major obstacles, and Elon Musk again mocked the plan.

There are some firmer signals. Nvidia shares were set to end a three-day losing streak on a report that ByteDance and Tencent have each received H200 chips, and reports say Samsung and SK hynix may unveil a very large multi-year investment plan. Apple's iPhone Duo is dominating headlines, with supply strain, delayed shipping dates and a battery figure now confirmed, while Apple's AI features are reportedly set for China in December.

editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as AI trade wobbles and iPhone Duo supply strains
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO of up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, and Microsoft has not commented. The report lands as investors grow wary of neocloud firms, and CoreWeave shares were marked down in coverage of the story.

The wider backdrop is a deepening selloff in US tech shares. Bloomberg reports that this is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI "picks and shovels" suppliers, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT also argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical constraints. Against that, SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in AI spending, are the next major read-across.

Apple dominated the rest of the day's flow. The iPhone Duo, its first foldable, is reportedly sold out into January, with staff told walk-in buyers are unlikely to get stock on launch day, and Gurman calls the staggered pre-order rollout a "major mistake". Apple's EU energy label put the device's battery at 4,883 mAh. Rumours also point to a touchscreen MacBook and a HomeView smart display with a robotic arm, with a possible retail refresh on 6 November. Most of these remain unconfirmed.

editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as iPhone Duo and AI trade wobble dominate
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. The report also points to grid connection delays and wider investor caution towards neocloud firms, with CoreWeave shares reported lower.

The wider backdrop is a jittery AI trade. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US technology shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, as rising financing costs could curb data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times asks whether Meta's earnings can restore confidence in AI investment, and a separate FT piece argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits. Against that, SemiAnalysis suggests more than 300 local data centre moratoriums have delayed only a small slice of US buildout.

Apple dominates the product news. Reports say the iPhone Duo foldable is sold out for months, that store staff have been told walk-in buyers should not expect stock, and that Apple's pre-order rollout across more than 70 countries was a mistake, according to Mark Gurman. Apple has also published the Duo's battery label, and a store refresh on 6 November is expected to coincide with new products including a touchscreen MacBook Pro. Most of these remain unconfirmed rumours.

top_stories.title: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale UK data centre before IPO
top_stories.summary: The Telegraph reports Microsoft has pulled out of anchoring Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, weeks before an IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and its Microsoft ties are strong. Microsoft has not commented, and grid delays are cited.

top_stories.title: AI trade reversal hits Asia's picks-and-shovels stocks
top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports a deepening US tech selloff is exposing weaknesses in Asia's AI supply chain. Higher financing costs could curb data-centre and hardware spending, putting regional supplier earnings at risk.

top_stories.title: Meta earnings seen as test of AI spending confidence
top_stories.summary: The FT previews whether Meta's results can restore faith in the AI investment boom. Investors will scrutinise the scale of its AI spending for signs of returns.

top_stories.title: America's roughly $10tn AI build-out meets physical limits
top_stories.summary: An FT analysis says data centres, power and equipment spending face real-world constraints. Combined with SemiAnalysis's finding that moratoriums have had little effect, the picture is one of bottlenecks rather than collapse.

top_stories.title: Gurman: Apple's iPhone Duo pre-order rollout was a major mistake
top_stories.summary: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman argues Apple opened pre-orders in more than 70 countries despite knowing supply was tight. Estimated shipping dates have slipped to around late January in most markets.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly standardises custom HBM base die on TSMC 3nm
top_stories.summary: A single unnamed report says Nvidia asked Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom memory base dies on TSMC's 3nm node, with Samsung reportedly accepting. The claimed gains are unverified.

top_stories.title: China may let big tech firms buy Nvidia H200 chips, capped
top_stories.summary: A Stocktwits report citing reports says Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek could be allowed to buy H200 chips, with tightly limited supply. It is unconfirmed but would be a limited easing of the chip trade.

rumour_watch.note: Seoul Economic Daily says Samsung may swap Snapdragon for Exynos in the Galaxy S27 Ultra over overheating; Qualcomm denies it, and the report rests on unnamed insiders, so treat as low-confidence.
A claimed 20% iPhone 18 Pro order cut with no named source or supply-chain detail; should be read as unverified until corroborated.
9to5Mac's touchscreen MacBook timing draws on Gurman, a well-sourced reporter, so a November launch is plausible, though Apple has not confirmed it.
A reported CFO-CEO rift over a 2026 OpenAI IPO comes via a thin Stocktwits summary with no sourcing, so it is weakly credible.

Stocktwits says Tesla may hold a public Cybercab launch in Austin in October; unconfirmed.
Bloomberg reports the EU has banned fashion brands from destroying unsold collections; scope and penalties unclear.
Reported FTC demands target OpenAI and Anthropic; the reports stress these are not findings of wrongdoing.
Anthropic backs a federal AI safety bill that would only allow blocking releases above $1bn damages or 50 deaths or injuries.
A second German court, in Aachen, has issued an injunction holding Google liable for false statements in its AI Mode answers.
Google DeepMind says four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft, including the Ender Dragon, with no human help.
A J.P. Morgan note suggests TSMC may bring 1.4nm mass production forward to H1 2028; analyst view, not confirmed.

Finance.title: France's protests hit bonds, stocks and the euro
Finance.notification: French bonds and the euro slide as weekend unrest rattles investors; markets also wary of AI and Iran.
Finance.summary:
The dominant market story is France. Violent weekend protests left public buildings burned and almost 2,400 people arrested, and on Monday French government bonds and stocks sold off. The 10-year yield rose 10 basis points to 4.89%, widening its spread over German Bunds, and the euro fell to a 17-month low against sterling. Analysts point to fiscal strain, a 2027 election and a deficit-cutting budget as added political risk. The unrest has spilled into other markets, with the French 10-year yield also cited in Wednesday's Asian coverage and the Cac 40 weighed by banks.

A second theme is the AI trade. Chipmakers and AI-linked stocks fell sharply in recent weeks, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 11.4% in one week and the Nasdaq 100 down 5.5%. Doubts about heavy borrowing, circular financing and a failed Australian datacentre listing have fuelled talk of a valuation reset. Sentiment bounced on Wednesday after SpaceX reported its first quarterly profit as a listed company and Elon Musk backed a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger, which is still only reported as under exploration.

Energy and geopolitics add pressure. Brent crude hovered near $110 a barrel amid Iran-related tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu is reported to be pushing to resume strikes on Iran. In the UK, vacancies fell, unemployment dipped to 4.7% and inflation is expected to rise to 3.4%, keeping the Bank of England's next move in focus.

points.text: UK vacancies fell 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, with small firms citing higher labour costs.
UK unemployment unexpectedly fell to 4.7%, seen as supporting a possible Bank of England rate hike in November.
South Korean regulators raise duplicate-listing concerns over SK hynix's planned Solidigm Nasdaq IPO; shares down over 30% in October.
A newly listed neocloud had a disastrous debut, reigniting fears that AI spending may be overheated.
Super Micro shares rose about 16% after preliminary quarterly sales beat forecasts, with revenue guidance well above consensus.
Reports say Chancellor John Healey has ruled out a capital gains tax rise before the 28 October Budget; a banking surcharge rise is discussed.

World.title: Unrest spreads across France as cost-of-living anger turns violent
World.notification: Weekend riots and looting across France test Lecornu's government as curfews spread and unions plan fresh protests.
World.summary:
Cost-of-living anger has turned into the most serious unrest in France for decades. Reports describe more than half a million people marching on Saturday, with masked activists and vandals joining in. About 1,500 shops and businesses were reportedly looted or destroyed, and around 1,000 police officers were injured. Curfews have been introduced in parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is meeting unions. Political blame is sharply divided, with the government pointing to the hard left and opposition figures accusing the prime minister of incompetence. A parliamentary inquiry has been proposed, and new protests are planned for 5 November, about six months before the presidential election. French equities and bonds have both been under pressure.

Across the Atlantic, the Canadian political scene drew attention as Alberta voters rejected separation. Preliminary results show roughly three-quarters backing unity, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said gives him a stronger hand in a trade dispute with the United States. The Canadian dollar and energy names were mixed. Oil markets remain sensitive to the Middle East, where Qatar reports progress in US-Iran talks, Tehran says it does not trust Washington, and the Strait of Hormuz remains largely disrupted.

Ukraine remains a live diplomatic and defence story. Zelenskyy says the US has resumed intelligence sharing after talks in Oslo, but he accuses the Pentagon of holding back interceptor deliveries that Europe has already paid for. Trump has urged Kyiv to make a deal, and envoy Steve Witkoff is due to meet Putin. Defence stocks have been mixed on the uncertainty.

points.text: Alberta voters rejected separation by about 76.5% in preliminary results; Smith says no referendum will be held during her term.
Independent MP Helen Haines is in critical but stable condition after an alleged car attack in Wangaratta; a 43-year-old man was arrested.
Four Canadian military members died and dozens were injured in a fire at CFB Wainwright; investigation may take a month.
Seven days of clashes in Tirana have left 295 injured, with protesters demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama resign.
A Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll puts Trump's approval at a record low of 33%, with 66% disapproving.
UK to deploy RAF Typhoons to Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi drones and missiles; no offensive strikes planned.

Tech.title: AI cloud deal talks and Big Tech rumours dominate tech
Tech.notification: Anthropic and Nscale reportedly in talks on a $45bn AI cloud deal. Nothing agreed yet.
Tech.summary:
The biggest theme today is the AI infrastructure boom and the strains showing around it. Bloomberg, Reuters and others report that Anthropic and Nscale are in talks on a compute deal worth about $45 billion, while Nvidia is reportedly in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid after its IPO was abandoned. Supermicro's preliminary figures show quarterly revenue well above guidance, but CoreWeave shares fell below $60 as a further GPU price rise and rate-hike worries hit borrowing-heavy neocloud firms. Utilities are also tightening rules on data centre connections, with Wood Mackenzie expecting only about 28% of requested grid capacity to be served.

Elsewhere, Microsoft's next Xbox plans dominate gaming news. Fortune's reporting, which Microsoft has not confirmed, suggests a handheld in 2027, a Project Helix console in 2028 priced at $1,200 to $1,800 internally, and a possible à la carte Game Pass. Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to explore a merger, which Elon Musk says carries no guarantee. Anthropic's IPO preparations also surfaced through reports on Eric Schmidt's stake and a draft safety bill.

Much of the day's material is rumour or unconfirmed, so the key figures should be treated cautiously until companies comment. Confirmed news is more limited, led by Supermicro's guidance raise and Arm's benchmark claims.

points.text: Reported Project Helix pricing and 2027 handheld timing point to a costly Xbox roadmap; Microsoft has not confirmed.
Supermicro expects quarterly revenue of $18.5bn to $19.5bn, above guidance, though its auditor has not reviewed the figures.
CoreWeave fell below $60 after a reported further 10% GPU price rise and rising Fed rate-hike expectations.
US utilities are demanding collateral and longer contracts to weed out speculative data centre projects.
Taction asked a judge for extra damages after a record $5.7bn jury verdict against Apple, which denies wrongdoing.
Google says four Gemini 4 agents completed Minecraft autonomously in 27 hours, at an estimated cost of $810 to $1,620.

Fashion.title: Looting hits Paris luxury stores as European protests spread
Fashion.notification: Paris luxury boutiques were looted in the 17-18 October protests, and more unrest is planned across Europe.
Fashion.summary:
The most urgent story is the unrest in France and wider Europe. Hundreds of stores in Paris and other French cities were looted on 17 and 18 October during cost-of-living and inequality protests, with luxury names including Saint Laurent, Celine, Dior and Louis Vuitton affected. Milan stores have closed, troops have been deployed ahead of planned protests, and similar unrest has been reported in Spain, Belgium and Portugal. Retailers are adding closures and security, and the French government has asked resale platforms to remove stolen goods.

The fallout is also visible in the business news. Ferragamo reported third-quarter revenue down 3.5% to €207 million, blaming geopolitical unrest and weaker summer demand, while its wholesale business fell sharply. Its turnaround is expected to be gradual, with store closures in lower-tier Chinese cities and a push into e-commerce. Luxury marketing is also in focus, with analysis suggesting brands are becoming more restrained.

Creative and cultural news continued across the sector. Dior is staging a Harrods pop-up featuring Jonathan Anderson's first cruise collection, Zane Li of Lii won the 2026 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, and Longchamp's Le Pliage tote shows the accessible-luxury model still working. Fashion weeks in New York, Tokyo, Mexico and Shanghai offered further runway talking points.

points.text: Ferragamo's third-quarter revenue fell 3.5% to €207 million, with wholesale weakness and slowing China sales.
Christina Nadin walked the 2026 Victoria's Secret Fashion Show, with the brand's repositioning under scrutiny.
Dior opens a Harrods holiday pop-up from 6 November to 27 December showing Jonathan Anderson's cruise pieces.
Longchamp's CEO forecasts double-digit growth in 2026 after 2025 sales rose 10%, with North America up 40%.
Buccellati opens a Florence boutique on Via Tornabuoni, its fifth Italian store, part of Richemont.
